title: How do you work with compound growth and CAGR without a calculator?
description: Compound growth explained for case interviews: CAGR, quick multipliers, the rule of 72, and a table of growth factors you can memorise.
hook: Growth over several years compounds, and simple approximations are usually good enough in an interview, as long as you know which ones to use. Here is a toolkit for compound growth without a calculator.
body:
The idea

Growing 10% a year for two years is not 20% in total; it is 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21, or 21%. Each year grows on top of the last.

Growth factors worth memorising

Yearly growthAfter 3 yearsAfter 5 years
5%×1.16×1.28
10%×1.33×1.61
15%×1.52×2.01
20%×1.73×2.49

Working out CAGR

Revenue grew from £100M to £161M in five years. From the table, ×1.61 over five years is about 10% a year. Without a table, guess a round rate, test it, and adjust (see the growth trick).

The rule of 72

Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ growth rate. At 8%, about 9 years. At 12%, about 6. It also works backwards: to double in 4 years, you need about 18% a year.

Common mistakes

  • Dividing total growth by the number of years.
  • Forgetting that a 50% fall needs a 100% rise to recover.

Use growth factors, not a straight-line average

Revenue grows from £100 million to £133.1 million in three years. The total increase is 33.1%, but dividing 33.1% by three is not the compound annual growth rate (CAGR). Instead solve £100m × (1 + g)^3 = £133.1m. Since 1.10³ = 1.331, the CAGR is 10%.

Why does this matter? A company growing 10% a year gains £10 million in year one, £11 million in year two and £12.1 million in year three. Each period grows on the previous total. Linear averaging understates the compounding effect when you are using it to forecast future revenue, capacity or customer counts.

For quick estimation, know a few factors: 5% annual growth for three years is roughly 1.16 times, 10% is about 1.33 times, and 20% is about 1.73 times. If the exact calculation is awkward, state an approximate CAGR and test it by multiplying the factor back. Do not pretend a rough mental estimate is precise.

In a growth case, also ask whether the historical CAGR is sustainable. Revenue may have risen because of one acquisition or an exceptional year. Separate organic growth, price and volume changes, and acquired sales before extrapolating a trend. A clean calculation is necessary, but the quality of the forecast rests on the assumptions.
